passages.original: sarem, si meum esset exemplum: sic scribit Catullus, sic
passages.english: [I would ex]cuse [it], if the precedent were my own: this is how Catullus writes, this is how
passages.notes: Fragment from the prose preface to Book 1 of Martial. 'sarem' is the end of a word broken off at the start of the passage, most likely 'excusarem' ('I would excuse [it]'). The sentence is incomplete at both ends.

passages.original: Gellius aedificat semper: modo limina ponit,
passages.english: Gellius is always building: now he is laying thresholds,
passages.notes: A single verse line; the sentence continues beyond the passage.

passages.english: You would be more learned, and chaste [too], Sappho:
passages.notes: The line is a fragment of a longer sentence. The condition behind 'would be' is not given in the passage, and no context is supplied. 'Doctior' (more learned) is comparative, while 'pudica' (chaste) is a plain adjective; the point seems to be that Sappho would become both more learned and chaste.

passages.original: Quod nec Vergilius nec carmine dicit Homerus,
passages.english: What neither Virgil nor Homer tells in song,
passages.notes: A single verse line; the sentence is incomplete.

passages.original: Lodices mittet docti tibi terra Catulli:
passages.english: The land of learned Catullus will send you blankets:
passages.notes: A single verse line from the Apophoreta (Book 14). The land of Catullus is Verona. 'Lodices' are blankets or coverlets.
